items.title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
items.summary: An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve. starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.Vercel AgentFor a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and , then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.build logsAccess is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with . Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.read:Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the , so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.user’s existing permissionsThe Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.The credential used depends on the work:The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in  applies to that repository even if the user also has access to . Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.acme/storefrontacme/paymentsA proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog.
